title: Chapter 57 — Of Whales in Paint; in Teeth; in Wood; in Sheet-Iron; in
paragraphs: On Tower Hill, as you go down to the London docks, you may have seen a crippled beggar holding up a painted board before him, depicting the tragic scene in which he lost his leg. There are three whales and three boats. And one of the boats — presumably the one containing the leg in all its original wholeness — is being crunched by the jaws of the front whale. For these ten years, they tell me, that man has held up that picture and displayed that stump to an incredulous world.

Throughout the Pacific, and also in Nantucket, and New Bedford, and Sag Harbor, you will come across lively sketches of whales and whaling-scenes, carved by the fishermen themselves on Sperm Whale teeth, or ladies' corset-stays carved out of Right Whale bone, and other like scrimshaw articles, as the whalemen call the numerous little ingenious objects they elaborately carve out of the raw material during their hours of ocean leisure. Some of them carry little boxes of dental-looking tools. The work they produce is remarkable.

Long exile from civilization inevitably restores a man to that condition in which God placed him — that is, what is called savagery. Your true whale-hunter is as much a savage as an Iroquois. I myself am a savage, owing allegiance to no one but the King of the Cannibals — and ready at any moment to rebel against him.

Now, one of the peculiar characteristics of the savage in his domestic hours is his wonderful patience and industry. An ancient Hawaiian war-club or spear-paddle, in its full complexity and elaboration of carving, is as great a testament to human perseverance as a Latin dictionary. For with nothing but a bit of broken sea-shell or a shark's tooth, that miraculous intricacy of wooden net-work has been achieved. And it has cost steady years of steady work.

As with the Hawaiian savage, so with the white sailor-savage. With the same marvelous patience, and with the same single shark's tooth of his one poor jackknife, he will carve you a bit of bone sculpture — not quite as expertly made, but as densely packed in its maze-like design as the Greek savage Achilles's shield, and full of wild spirit and suggestion, as the prints of that fine old Dutch savage, Albrecht Durer.

Wooden whales, or whales cut in profile out of the small dark slabs of the noble South Sea war-wood, are frequently found in the forecastles of American whalers. Some of them are carved with considerable accuracy.

At some old gable-roofed country houses you will see brass whales hung by the tail as door knockers. When the porter is sleepy, the anvil-headed whale would work best. But these knocking whales are seldom noteworthy as faithful likenesses. On the steeples of some old-fashioned churches you will see sheet-iron whales placed there as weather-vanes. But they are so high up, and besides are practically labeled "Hands off!" so you cannot examine them closely enough to form any real opinion.

In bony, rocky regions of the earth, where at the base of high broken cliffs masses of rock lie strewn in fantastic groupings upon the plain, you will often discover shapes like the petrified forms of whales partly merged in grass, which on a windy day breaks against them in a surf of green waves.

Then again, in mountainous countries where the traveler is continually surrounded by amphitheater-like heights, here and there from some lucky vantage point you will catch passing glimpses of whale-shaped profiles defined along the undulating ridges. But you must be a thorough whaleman to see these sights. And not only that — if you wish to return to such a sight, you must be sure to take the exact latitude and longitude of your first viewpoint, or the chance-like nature of these formations may mean you never find the same one again.

Nor, when your imagination is expanded and lifted by your subject, can you fail to trace out great whales in the starry heavens, and boats in pursuit of them — as when, long filled with thoughts of war, the Eastern nations saw armies locked in battle among the clouds. Thus at the North I have chased Leviathan round and round the Pole with the revolutions of the bright stars that first outlined him for me. And beneath the brilliant Antarctic skies I have boarded the constellation Argo-Navis and joined the chase against the starry Cetus far beyond.

With a frigate's anchors for my bridle-bits and bundles of harpoons for spurs, I wish I could mount that whale and leap the topmost skies, to see whether the fabled heavens with all their countless tents really lie encamped beyond my mortal sight!
